name: All Day Music
editorial_article: "All Day Music" is the titular opening track of the 1971 studio album by the American funk band War. Released as a single in July 1971, this track serves as a quintessential example of the group’s transition into their own distinct sound following their early collaborations with Eric Burdon. The song is a masterclass in the "slow groove" style that characterized the band’s identity, blending soul, Latin-influenced percussion, and psychedelic rock sensibilities into a cohesive, atmospheric whole. \n\nComposed by Jerry Goldstein and the members of War, the track showcases the group's democratic musical approach, with prominent roles for Lonnie Jordan’s organ, Lee Oskar’s harmonica, and the heavy, rhythmic interplay between the bass and congas. It captures the essence of the band's aesthetic during the early 70s—a period marked by artistic independence and critical acclaim. The track, along with its album, helped define the genre of progressive soul, moving away from the conventional structures of rock and R&B to favor longer, exploratory grooves that emphasized atmosphere and rhythmic complexity. Its relaxed yet driving tempo remains a hallmark of War’s legacy, influencing generations of funk and soul musicians. By the time it was released, War had firmly established themselves as a formidable creative force, and "All Day Music" stands as a foundational document of that pivotal era.
editorial_teaser: The titular track from War's 1971 album, "All Day Music" is a definitive slow-groove funk anthem that highlights the band's signature blend of rhythmic soul and Latin-infused textures.
